senses.definition: A holiday, festival, especially a religious one

quotes.text: The seventh day shall be a feast to the Lord.
quotes.reference: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London: […] Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Exodus 13:6:

quotes.text: Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the feast of the passover.
quotes.reference: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London: […] Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Luke 2:41:

senses.definition: A very large meal, often of a ceremonial nature.
examples: We had a feast to celebrate the harvest.
It was a feast for the eyes.

senses.definition: (intransitive) To partake in a feast, or large meal.
examples: I feasted on turkey and dumplings.

quotes.text: With my love's picture then my eye doth feast.
quotes.reference: 1609, William Shakespeare, “Sonnet 47”, in Shake-speares Sonnets. […], London: By G[eorge] Eld for T[homas] T[horpe] and are to be sold by William Aspley, →OCLC:

senses.definition: (transitive) To hold a feast in honor of (someone).
examples: We feasted them after the victory.

quotes.text:
He that shall see this day, and live old age,
Will yearly on the vigil feast his neighbors
And say “Tomorrow is Saint Crispian.”
quotes.reference: 1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life of Henry the Fift”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London: […] Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene iii]:

quotes.text: His ancestor, he said, had been feasted there, when he went forward with the then Lord Ravenswood to the fatal battle of Flodden, in which they both fell.
